summary: Broad 2023–2026 wearable fall-detection landscape survey (19 sources, grouped by sensor modality / computational model / edge-cloud deployment) for thesis Ch1-2 related work. Anchored on a Feb-2026 PRISMA systematic review (130 studies, IEEE Xplore/PubMed/Scopus) giving quotable accuracy-by-modality ranges. Surfaces several ESP32/MCU-class CNN systems directly comparable to SPARK's own INT8 model, and a field-wide simulated-vs-real-world validation gap that independently corroborates Tracks 8/9.
result_text:
### Research question
Broad, systematic-review-style landscape of wearable fall-detection systems, 2023–2026: sensor modalities, ML approaches, edge-vs-cloud deployment trends, and reported performance ranges — to ground thesis Ch.2 related-work, distinct from Tracks 1/2's narrow novelty-claim prior-art hunts.

### Bottom line
The field has consolidated around IMU-wearable + deep learning (CNN/LSTM/Transformer) as the dominant paradigm, reporting 90–99.9% accuracy on curated/simulated benchmarks, with a fast-growing TinyML/MCU-class sub-literature (ESP32/Arduino, <20KB models, <40ms inference) directly comparable to SPARK's own architecture. The single most important cross-cutting finding is methodological, not technical: the large majority of this literature (≈98.5% in the most rigorous recent count) validates only on simulated falls, almost never on real-world unanticipated falls in the target elderly population — a limitation SPARK shares via SisFall and one Tracks 8/9 already examined in SPARK-specific depth. Existing NLM notebook sources (SisFall paper, WHO falls report, 2 threshold-algorithm papers, TFLite-Micro paper, Nepal census) are foundational/context sources, not 2023–2026 landscape papers, so nothing below duplicates them.

### Key findings

**Finding 1 — Sensor-modality landscape and reported accuracy ranges are now well quantified.**
- Evidence: A Feb-2026 PRISMA systematic review (130 studies, searched IEEE Xplore/PubMed/Scopus, Jan 2008–May 2025) found wearable/IMU systems are the most-studied modality (36.2%), followed by vision (20.8%), then ambient RF (radar/WiFi/LiDAR) and hybrid fusion. Its Table 3 reports accuracy ranges by modality: Wearable IMU/accelerometer 90.3–99.9%; Vision (RGB/RGB-D) 79.6–99.98%; Ambient radar/RF 90(recall)–99.77%; Ambient-other (PIR/smart-flooring) 93–99%; Hybrid/multimodal up to 100% in-lab.
- Source: Ishaq, Guastella, Sutera & Muscato (2026), *Applied Sciences* 16(4):1929.
- Confidence: Established (full text read; PRISMA methodology, formal multi-database search).
- Relevance to SPARK: Gives Ch.2 a directly citable, current "reported performance ranges" figure. SPARK's wrist-IMU choice sits in the best-populated, best-evidenced modality band — but accuracy ranges alone don't obviously favor wearables over ambient/radar (comparable or higher ceilings), so Ch.1's rationale for wearables should lean on cost/no-install/elderly-compliance/Nepal-affordability rather than accuracy superiority.

**Finding 2 — Deep learning has displaced classical ML as the dominant computational paradigm since ~2021.**
- Evidence: Same review's period analysis: 2008–2015 threshold/classical-ML era; 2016–2020 near-even split (classical ML n=23 vs DL n=21); 2021–2025 DL dominant (n=41) vs classical ML (n=9), threshold-based nearly displaced. CNN, LSTM/GRU, CNN-LSTM hybrids, and Transformers are the reported architecture families.
- Source: Ishaq et al. (2026), §3.2 / Fig. 6.
- Confidence: Established.
- Relevance to SPARK: SPARK's 1D CNN (Layer 2) is squarely in the current mainstream approach — good positioning evidence for Ch.2. SPARK's own classical-ML Stage 2 (RF/XGBoost, per §2.4 of the tracker) is now a minority approach in the field; Ch.2/Ch.4 should frame it explicitly as an interpretability/assignment baseline rather than the claimed contribution, consistent with the field's own trajectory.

**Finding 3 — A concrete, current TinyML/MCU-class sub-literature exists and is directly size/latency-comparable to SPARK.**
- Evidence: MicroFallNet (FireModel/SqueezeNet-derived CNN) reports 97.91%/97.86% geometric-mean accuracy on UMAFALL/FallAllD, 89.75% parameter reduction, 30.3ms inference on an ESP32 smart wristband. A separate dual-IMU (waist+thigh) TinyCNN system deploys on Arduino Nano BLE 33 Sense with BLE alerting. Duan et al. (2026) report a CNN-LSTM achieving 99.3% accuracy/98.97% F1 on KFall (LOSO validation) and, notably, zero-shot cross-dataset transfer to **SisFall** — SPARK's own primary dataset — at 98.3% accuracy/97.9% F1 (~1% degradation).
- Source: MicroFallNet, *Pervasive and Mobile Computing* (2025); "A practical wearable fall detection system based on tiny convolutional neural networks," *Biomedical Signal Processing and Control* (2023); Duan, Minh, Dung & Linh, *Int. J. Technology* 17(3):919–935 (2026).
- Confidence: Established for each paper's own reported numbers; Supported inference that these are meaningfully comparable to SPARK (datasets/protocols differ — see Contradictions).
- Relevance to SPARK: These are the closest published analogues to SPARK's actual deployment target (MCU-class, kB-scale, sub-40ms). SPARK's current 87.81% tuned sensitivity / 0.9185 AUC-ROC (tracker v51) sits below several of these — independent, literature-side corroboration (distinct from Track 4's technique-focused literature) that the sensitivity gap to the ≥90%/≥90% WP2 target is real and worth closing before Oct 31, 2026. The Duan et al. SisFall cross-dataset number is a useful direct comparison point for Ch.5.

**Finding 4 — Classical-ML (RF/SVM/XGBoost) wearable fall detection remains an active, if shrinking, sub-literature with concrete comparison numbers.**
- Evidence: An optimized Random Forest classifier (feature engineering + Grid/Randomized Search) reports 92% accuracy/91% precision/89% recall/90% F1 at 0.045s/prediction, targeted at smartwatch deployment. A 2025 sensor-fusion study compares RF, SVM, XGBoost, logistic regression, and a majority-voter ensemble on accelerometer+barometric-altimeter features. A deep-forest (cascaded RF) IoT framework is evaluated on the SmartFall dataset.
- Source: Afuan & Isnanto, *J. Applied Data Sciences* 6(1):213–224 (2025); *Sensors* 25(23):7220 (2025); *Computer Systems Science and Engineering* 45(3):2377–2389 (2023).
- Confidence: Established.
- Relevance to SPARK: Direct benchmark set for SPARK's own Stage-2 RF/XGBoost baseline (tracker notes this notebook has "never [been] executed") once it is actually run — gives Ch.4/5 real comparison numbers rather than an unbenchmarked baseline claim.

**Finding 5 — Edge/mobile-edge-computing architectures (vs. cloud) are an active, quantified research direction, and recent reviews explicitly recommend local processing.**
- Evidence: A multilayer mobile-edge-computing (MEC) system with knowledge distillation reports knowledge distillation improving front-end accuracy by 11.65% on **SisFall** and 2.78% on FallAllD, while cutting data latency 46.67% (SisFall) and 54.15% (FallAllD), versus MEC without distillation. Separately, the Ishaq et al. (2026) review's Discussion explicitly argues future systems should "ensure that video/sensitive data is processed at the edge... so sensitive footage never leaves the user's local network," citing GDPR-style consent obligations.
- Source: Mao, Wang, Chou, Liu & Tsao, "MECKD," *IEEE Sensors Journal* 24(24):42195–42209 (2024); Ishaq et al. (2026), §4 Discussion.
- Confidence: Established (MECKD numbers); Supported inference that this generically validates SPARK's specific architecture (the review does not evaluate SPARK; it's a field-level normative recommendation, not evidence *of* SPARK).
- Relevance to SPARK: Independent, broad-literature support for SPARK's local-gateway/non-cloud design decision (complementary to, not a substitute for, Track 1's narrower IEEE/Scopus novelty-specific search on the two-stage gated architecture itself). MECKD's use of SisFall is also a second direct-dataset comparison point worth flagging to whoever benchmarks SPARK's gateway pipeline.

**Finding 6 — Ambient/RF/vision modalities remain a large, separate, and competitive literature (landscape-completeness, not a SPARK design input).**
- Evidence: Multiple 2023–2025 IEEE-indexed works on radar (mmWave/FMCW/CW Doppler), WiFi CSI, and vision/skeleton-based (CNN, Transformer, GCN) fall detection, including a dedicated IEEE Robotics & Automation Magazine survey of radar-based fall detection (2024) and a 2025 Sensors review of ambient-assisted-living/smart-home fall detection performance.
- Source: Hu et al., "Radar-based fall detection: A survey," *IEEE Robotics & Automation Magazine* (2024, cited via secondary reference list — see Sources); Kittiyanpunya et al., *IEEE Access* (2023); Benkaci et al., *Procedia Computer Science* 241:203–211 (2024); Gorce & Jacquier-Bret, *Sensors* (2025).
- Confidence: Established for existence/general findings; Medium confidence on exact bibliographic detail for the radar survey and the millimeter-wave paper (chained through a secondary reference list, not independently opened this session — flagged in Sources).
- Relevance to SPARK: Useful only for Ch.1's "gap" framing (why wearable vs. ambient) and completeness of the "grouped by approach" landscape Track 16 was asked to produce. Not a design input — Track 17 already covers the commercial-product angle of this same non-wearable landscape.

**Finding 7 — The field has a well-documented, quantified simulated-vs-real-world validation gap, which is the main reason reported performance ranges vary so widely.**
- Evidence: The Ishaq et al. (2026) review found that of 130 detection-focused older-adult fall studies, 98.5% validated only on simulated falls by volunteers (often young/healthy); only 2 studies (1.5%) validated against real-world, unanticipated falls in the actual target elderly population. A separate 2025 systematic study on commodity wearable devices independently reports that of ≥57 wearable fall-detection projects surveyed, only 7.1% tested in real-world settings. A foundational 2022 comparison of real-world vs. simulated fall datasets found real and "fake" (acted) falls can differ kinematically more than fake falls differ from ordinary daily activities, and that clinical trials show detectors underperforming their reported lab accuracy once deployed.
- Source: Ishaq et al. (2026), §3.3/§4; "Enhancing Real-World Fall Detection Using Commodity Devices," *Sensors* 25(17):5249 (2025); Casilari & Silva, *Measurement* 202:111843 (2022).
- Confidence: Established — three independent sources converge on the same qualitative conclusion, though they use different study counts/denominators (see Contradictions).
- Relevance to SPARK: This is a field-wide, not SPARK-specific, weakness — SPARK's current pipeline is likewise 100% SisFall (simulated). This finding *independently corroborates*, from the broad literature rather than SPARK-specific investigation, the exact concern Tracks 8 and 9 already investigated directly (elderly-vs-young fall kinematics and self-collected sample-size adequacy respectively). Recommend Ch.1/Ch.2 state this as a known, field-wide limitation candidly rather than leaving it implicit — doing so is a defensible, literature-grounded framing for a thesis defence panel, and pairs naturally with Tracks 8/9's SPARK-specific findings when the orchestrator synthesizes across tracks.

**Finding 8 — Explainability (XAI) is explicitly flagged as an underexplored gap in the current broad literature.**
- Evidence: The Ishaq et al. (2026) review states current literature "lacks sufficient focus on Explainable AI (XAI) approaches, such as SHAP," and that this limits clinical trust/adoption.
- Source: Ishaq et al. (2026), §4 Discussion.
- Confidence: Established (explicit reviewer statement, one source).
- Relevance to SPARK: Landscape-level corroboration for Novelty Claim 3's positioning (local SHAP explainability). This is deliberately a light touch — the narrow IEEE/Scopus-specific SHAP prior-art search is Track 2's completed job; this finding is only cited here as broad Ch.2 framing context, not a re-litigation of Track 2's narrowing recommendation.

### Contradictions and limitations
- **Dataset/protocol heterogeneity blocks apples-to-apples comparison.** Ishaq et al. (2026) themselves state a quantitative meta-analysis was "not feasible" due to heterogeneity in sensor modality, validation protocol, and population across the 130 studies. The MCU-comparable numbers in Finding 3 use UMAFALL/FallAllD/KFall, not SisFall directly (except Duan et al.'s zero-shot transfer number) — treat these as informative context, not a strict leaderboard against SPARK's own 87.81%/0.9185 AUC-ROC.
- **Different "real-world validation" denominators.** The 98.5%/1.5% figure (130 older-adult-focused studies, PRISMA-screened) and the 7.1% figure (57 wearable-specific projects, different inclusion criteria) are not the same count and shouldn't be quoted as if interchangeable — they are two independently-sourced measures that happen to converge qualitatively, not one statistic.
- **Preprint/secondary-source caveats.** MECKD's IEEE Sensors Journal publication is confirmed via cross-referencing three independent copies (IEEE Xplore listing, arXiv preprint with matching abstract, academia.edu with matching author list) — high confidence. By contrast, the radar survey (Hu et al., *IEEE RAM*), the millimeter-wave paper (Kittiyanpunya et al.), TinyCNN (Yu et al. 2023), and both Al-Qaness et al. papers were found only via secondary reference lists inside other papers, not opened directly this session — bibliographic detail (exact authors/volume/pages) for these should be re-verified before final thesis citation.
- **Scope boundary with Track 1.** This track deliberately did not run a formal IEEE Xplore/Scopus query narrowly targeted at "MCU-class two-stage gated pipelines" — that is Action #26/Track 1's specific job (still **pending/unclaimed** as of this checkpoint). Finding 3/5 here are broad-landscape context, not a substitute for that narrower search.

### Recommendation
1. Use this 19-source set, organized by the same grouping used above (modality → computational model → MCU/edge deployment → classical-ML baseline → edge-vs-cloud → validation methodology), as the draft skeleton for thesis Ch.2's related-work section.
2. Cite Ishaq et al. (2026) Table 3 as the headline "reported performance ranges" figure — it's the most current, most rigorously-sourced (PRISMA, IEEE Xplore/PubMed/Scopus, 130 studies) single citation available.
3. Flag to Aaradhya: the MCU-class literature comparison (Finding 3) independently suggests SPARK's current 87.81% sensitivity has room to close before the Oct 31 WP2 gate — this is a second, literature-grounded signal alongside Track 4's technique-focused findings, not a duplicate of it.
4. When the orchestrator runs cross-track synthesis, pair Finding 7 (field-wide sim-vs-real gap) explicitly with Tracks 8 and 9's SPARK-specific findings — together they make a stronger, better-sourced limitations paragraph than either alone.
5. Before final thesis submission, independently re-verify the four secondary-chained citations flagged above (Hu et al. radar survey, Kittiyanpunya et al., Yu et al. TinyCNN, both Al-Qaness et al. papers) by opening their primary sources directly.
6. Track 1 (task_2026-08-21_002) is still unclaimed — the narrow IEEE/Scopus query Action #26 needs remains outstanding and isn't covered by this broad-survey track.
